WRAPUP 3-Trump says he is highly unlikely to order Iran strikes if talks progress US President Donald Trump said on Sunday he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progress, even as both countries reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters | Updated: 09-11-2026 05:45 IST | Created: 09-11-2026 05:45 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump said on Sunday he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progress, even as both countries reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz. "It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," Trump told CNN in a phone interview. "The answer is, highly unlikely it's going to be necessary." CNN did not specify exactly what it had asked Trump, who also said that if strikes resume, the US has identified potential infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges "that we can knock down in literally one hour." Later on Sunday afternoon, Trump posted on Truth Social that "Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect" on Iran. The campaign, first reported by Reuters on Saturday, will crack down on Tehran's movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material over its land borders and through the Caspian Sea. Trump acknowledged after the last week's US midterm elections that the Iran war was a part of the reason for Republicans' defeat, while Vice President JD Vance, seen as a potential successor to Trump when his term ends in two years, went a step further, saying definitively in a social media post, "The reason we lost is the war." Trump told reporters on Sunday that "a lot of people did not like Vance's comments on Iran." Secretary of State Marco Rubio, widely considered another contender to succeed Trump, declined to comment on Sunday on a link between the war and the elections. "All I can tell you is that the president of the United States identified a very real threat to this country that existed for a very long period of time, and he addressed it," Rubio told reporters. Asked separately about diplomatic efforts to end the war, Rubio said he did not believe a breakthrough was imminent. "The president would always prefer to solve this and every problem diplomatically. Sometimes that's not possible, unfortunately. But if there's a chance to do it. We'll explore it. Right now, it hasn't been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic," Rubio said. Trump had been hinting that he would renew major attacks on Iran once the elections were over, but there has been no sign of a large-scale US military operation. Iran has said it would respond by striking US and Israeli targets. Iranian media suggested that explosions in southern Iran on Saturday were related to Iranian military activities rather than US strikes. Iran's state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory following blasts heard in several areas, including on Qeshm Island in the strait. Both the US and Iran have continued strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, restricting exports of energy and other commodities vital to the world economy. Iran's state television said the evening explosions might be related to Iranian military activity in the waterway, where Iran said two vessels had hit mines and a third had caught fire. The US said its air force had disabled a vessel in the Gulf of Oman beyond the strait. Tasnim news agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage. Neither Iran nor the US has commented on that report. Washington said on November 2 that it had struck the island in a limited defensive measure against Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets. COMMERCIAL VESSEL, OIL TANKERS HIT Since the US and Israel began attacks on Iran in February, Tehran has sought the upper hand by hitting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz to block Gulf energy exports, while US forces began blockading movements to and from Iranian ports in April. The US military said on Saturday evening that its air force had fired at the stern of a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, disabling it as it tried to get through the blockade. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two oil tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to pass through an "unauthorized route" in the Strait of Hormuz. A third tanker had also suffered an explosion and caught fire, the semi-official Fars news agency reported later. Reuters was not able to confirm any of the reported strikes. Monitors from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said a bulk carrier and military forces were involved in an incident in the Gulf of Oman, approximately 18 nautical miles east of the United Arab Emirates' city of Khor Fakkan, with damage unknown. It was unclear if it was related to the reported US attack. A conflict between Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia has escalated this month, enlarging the wider Middle East war. On Sunday, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said an administrative building belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco in Riyadh had been damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries or fatalities reported. Qatar, which has been mediating in talks to try to end a conflict that has shaken the world economy, on Saturday denied reports that the US and Iran had failed to reach a deal. The Qatari prime minister had affirmed that both sides were continuing to work toward an agreement, it said. Iran has submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday, saying the US was reviewing it but discussions would depend on Washington first meeting Tehran's seven demands. These include sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and war reparations, while Washington says nuclear issues must feature in initial talks.

Nvidia opens probe after report that CEO Huang was target of foreign intelligence Reuters | Updated: 09-11-2026 02:01 IST | Created: 09-11-2026 02:01 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Nvidia said on Sunday that it is initiating an independent investigation after a media report that founder and CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Top Republican lawmakers in the US House of Representatives have called on Huang to brief Congress this month about a New York Times report in October alleging he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. The company said on Sunday that, while its board has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information. Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added. Axios reported on Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full responsibility for his actions. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang said in the draft email seen by Reuters. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.

item.content:encoded:
X says police order demanding removal of Indian free-speech groups' accounts was fake Reuters | Updated: 06-11-2026 12:37 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 12:37 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Police orders asking X to block online accounts of two of India's most prominent free speech groups were fake, the social media company told an Indian court on Friday, days after the purported content removal requests sparked a public outcry. The orders, submitted through X's online reporting form in the name of a senior Delhi police officer, sought the removal of the accounts of the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and the Software Freedom Law Centre, India (SFLC.in), claiming they had defamed the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the Hindu nationalist group from which Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party emerged. "It turns out this was somebody playing an impostor, somebody impersonating Delhi police who has sent this," a lawyer for X told the Delhi High Court, saying the company had conducted an internal investigation. Delhi police did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Free-speech activists have repeatedly said that India's strict content removal regulations are a way to curb dissent in the world's most populous nation. India, which has more than 1.1 billion internet subscribers, says the directives target unlawful or misleading content and respect lawful expression. The purported takedown orders invoked Indian rules that require platforms to act on the notices within three hours. X forwarded them to the affected users before establishing that they were fake. IFF had asked the court to quash the orders, which sparked an uproar on social media this week, with Amnesty and India's main opposition party contesting their legality. The groups also received legal notices last week, purportedly on behalf of the RSS, that demanded they stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders, according to the petition.

item.title: Trump questions Russian fuel ban, signals no change

item.content:encoded:
Trump questions Russian fuel ban, signals no change President Donald Trump questioned the US law banning Russian petroleum imports, stating he would review it, though no policy change was announced amid a dispute over his administration's authorisation of Russian diesel transactions. ANI | Updated: 06-11-2026 10:05 IST | Created: 06-11-2026 10:05 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

President Donald Trump has cast doubt on the US law banning Russian petroleum imports, indicating that he would review the legislation while declaring no policy change amid mounting controversy surrounding his administration’s clearance of Russian diesel transactions. “That probably makes it a pretty bad law. I'll take a look at it, sure,” Trump stated after a journalist informed him that the measure had been enacted by Congress and signed by President Joe Biden in 2022. During his interaction in the Oval Office, the reporter raised questions regarding a vessel transporting Russian diesel across the ocean towards the United States, alongside the legal restrictions governing the offloading of its cargo. Initially, Trump questioned whether the restriction fell under the purview of the Jones Act, prompting the correspondent to clarify that the issue pertained to legislation passed in 2022. His response provided no timeline, proposed amendment or explanation regarding how the administration intended to reconcile its authorisation of diesel imports with the statutory import prohibition, nor did he declare that the ban had been lifted. This distinction remains critical, given that the Treasury had previously granted a separate authorisation roughly four weeks earlier. On October 9, the Office of Foreign Assets Control released General License 135, permitting financial dealings otherwise prohibited under two sets of Russia-related sanctions regulations whenever they involve the sale, delivery, offloading or importation of Russian-origin diesel. The document explicitly covers imports into the United States, with the waiver remaining in effect until 12.01 am Eastern Daylight Time on April 7, 2027. While exempting withdrawals from accounts maintained at US financial institutions belonging to Russia's central bank, National Wealth Fund or Finance Ministry, the licence specifically targets diesel rather than signalling a general reopening of trade encompassing all Russian petroleum products. Conversely, the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, formally approved on April 8, 2022, independently prohibits inbound shipments of Russian products listed under Chapter 27 of the US tariff schedule. The framework outlines a strict protocol for lifting this restriction, requiring presidential certification verifying an agreement accepted by Ukraine regarding Russia's withdrawal and a halt to hostilities, the elimination of any immediate Russian military threat directed at NATO members, and recognition of Ukrainian self-determination. Additionally, the requirement necessitates prior consultation with congressional committees, alongside a 90-day review period following certification before any cancellation takes effect, unless Congress passes a resolution of disapproval. The aforementioned Treasury licence, on its own, does not establish that this statutory process has been fulfilled. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill formally contested the approval through a November 2 letter addressed to port and terminal operators, just three days before Trump's recent comments. “The Trump Administration’s authorisation of Russian fuel imports directly conflicts with federal law,” she asserted. Sherrill contended that the legislation did not grant the executive branch blanket authority to set aside the prohibition through licences, cautioning commercial entities against accepting deliveries of the petroleum and vowing that New Jersey would deploy all available legal and regulatory measures to block such imports. (ANI)
